latin: Quid agis hodiē? Tempestāte<sup>1</sup> hāc serēnā jūcundum sit domō exīre.
Lūdīs et āthlēticīs nimis dēlectāris<sup>2</sup>, studia autem neglegis;
... incēpistī linguam latīnam discere, nōndum<sup>3</sup> tamen classicī auctōris operam<sup>4</sup> ūllam<sup>5</sup> lēgistī.
Quid ex mē quaeris? Prīmum linguam latīnam classicam intellegere nōn possum; deinde auctōrēs classicī taediōsī sunt; tum āerem pūrum dēsīderō<sup>6</sup>.

Bonitāte<sup>7</sup> āeris pūrī exceptā<sup>8</sup>, aliquantulum<sup>9</sup> errās: scrīpta simplicia linguae classicae jam intellegere possēs sī vellēs<sup>10</sup>... Ergō, sī vīs, crās incipiēmus...
ita cōnsuētūdinem<sup>11</sup> jungēmus cum auctōribus novīs et veteribus.
Placet<sup>12</sup>, sī taediōsōs vītāmus: etiam nostrā aetāte nōn dēsunt in omnibus linguīs auctōrēs quī intellegī<sup>13</sup> nōn possunt.
Nihil timuerīs! Multī sunt auctōrēs latīnī omnium generum: quod quaerimus, id haud<sup>14</sup> difficulter inveniēmus.
Tibi cōnfīdō. Sed prīmum eāmus ambulātum<sup>15</sup>!
latinAccented: Quid agis hódiē? Tempestā́te<sup>1</sup> hāc serḗnā jūcúndum sit domō exī́re.
Lūdīs et āthlḗticīs nimis dēlectā́ris<sup>2</sup>, stúdia autem néglegis;
... incēpístī linguam latī́nam díscere, nōndum<sup>3</sup> tamen clássicī auctṓris óperam<sup>4</sup> ūllam<sup>5</sup> lēgístī.
Quid ex mē quaeris? Prīmum linguam latī́nam clássicam intellégere nōn possum; deínde auctṓrēs clássicī taediṓsī sunt; tum āerem pūrum dēsī́derō<sup>6</sup>.

Bonitā́te<sup>7</sup> āeris pūrī excéptā<sup>8</sup>, aliquántulum<sup>9</sup> errās: scrīpta simplícia linguae clássicae jam intellégere possēs sī vellēs<sup>10</sup>... Ergō, sī vīs, crās incipiḗmus...
ita cōnsuētū́dinem<sup>11</sup> jungḗmus cum auctṓribus novīs et vetéribus.
Placet<sup>12</sup>, sī taediṓsōs vītā́mus: étiam nostrā aetā́te nōn dēsunt in ómnibus linguīs auctṓrēs quī intéllegī<sup>13</sup> nōn possunt.
Nihil timúerīs! Multī sunt auctṓrēs latī́nī ómnium génerum: quod quáerimus, id haud<sup>14</sup> difficúlter inveniḗmus.
Tibi cōnfī́dō. Sed prīmum eā́mus ambulā́tum<sup>15</sup>!
english: What are you doing today? In this [fine] (serene) weather it would be pleasant to go out of the house.
You [like] games and sports [too much] (by games and sports too much you are delighted), but you neglect [your] studies;
you have started learning Latin [and you have not yet read a single work by a classical author] (not-yet one-single work of-a-classical-author you have read).
What [are you asking of] me (from me)? First I cannot understand classical Latin; then the classical authors are boring; finally I [lack] fresh air.

[Apart from] the benefit(s) of fresh air (excepted), you are a little bit mistaken: you could already understand simple writings in classical Latin if you wanted to (but you don't)... So, if you want, we will begin tomorrow...
in this way we will make the acquaintance of recent and ancient authors.
[All right] (it pleases), if we avoid the bores: even in our time, in all languages, there is no lack of authors [who are incomprehensible] (who cannot be understood).
Don't be afraid (subj. pft) [of] anything! There are many Latin authors of all kinds: we will find what we are looking for [without difficulty] (not with-difficulty).
I trust you. But first let's go for a walk!

footnotes: Tempestas, -atis, f., the weather; sometimes the storm; tempus, -oris, n., time that passes; the same difference as in English between weather and time, or in German between Wetter and Zeit.

Delectaris: the passive turn is often preferred when it is a question of verbs of state (you are delighted by) rather than the active turn: ludos et athletica amas; besides, the verb amare applies rather to people than to things.
Opera, -ae, f., work (of art); opus, operis, n., work, labour; opus est + inf., it is necessary.
Ullus, -a, -um, any, is not negative in itself: the negation is already found in nondum; the use of the pronoun nullus, -a, -um, which is negative, would turn the sentence into an affirmation.
Desiderare, to feel the lack of something.

Bonitas, -atis, f., from bonus, -a, -um. From now on we will no longer indicate words in -tas, -tatis, f., which correspond to our words in -ty (French -té). Note that the correspondence is often clearer in form than in substance.
Excipio, -is, -ere, cepi, ceptum = ex + capio, to take out of, to withdraw, to except. Here in the ablative of the participle (ablative absolute).

Aliquantulum: we have seen quantus, -a, -um, how big; whence aliquantus, of a certain size; and its diminutive aliquantulus, of a certain size however small, that is to say of a certain smallness; used here adverbially.
Posses si velles: imperfect of the subjunctive corresponding to a conditional. This construction corresponds to the PRESENT UNREAL: you could (do it today) if you wanted to (but you don't want to).
Consuetudo, -inis, f., habit (L. 29, N. 13). Words in -do, -dinis are feminine; consuetudinem jungere, to form an acquaintance (that is to say habitual relations).
Placeo, -es, -ere, placui, v. i., to please. On a ballot paper (tessera, like a railway ticket) the inscription placet means YES (NON SE DIT veto, I forbid).
Haud is used in front of an adjective or an adverb in preference to non: it makes it possible to show unambiguously that THE NEGATION APPLIES TO THE WORD THAT FOLLOWS AND NOT TO THE WHOLE SENTENCE.

Ambulatum, is, we remind you, the supine of ambulare. The accusative of the supine in um is practically only used after verbs of motion: eo visum, I go to see. The ablative, which is in u, is only used after certain adjectives: horribile visu, horrible to see.
comments: Aequalis, -e, equal; here understood: in age. — Lapis, lapidis, m., stone, both the cut stone and the precious stone: do you know the noun and adjective LAPIDARY?
Our notes sometimes repeat themselves: that is because we are trying both to simplify your work and to make the important words well known to you.

latin: Māvult lūdere quam labōrāre. Māvult lūdum quam labōrem. Lūdum labōrī praefert.
Mēlius est lūdere cum tempestās serēna est et litterīs studēre cum pluit.
Sī tempestās serēna esset, tēcum folle libenter lūderem.
Placet, sed hodiē pluit lapidibus: librum legere mālō.
In bibliothēcam intrēmus! Ecce līber quem nunquam lēgistī!
latinAccented: Māvult lū́dere quam labōrā́re. Māvult lūdum quam labṓrem. Lūdum labṓrī praefert.
Mḗlius est lū́dere cum tempéstās serḗna est et lítterīs studḗre cum pluit.
Sī tempéstās serḗna esset, tēcum folle libénter lū́derem.
Placet, sed hódiē pluit lapídibus: librum légere mālō.
In bibliothḗcam intrḗmus! Ecce līber quem nunquam lēgístī!
english: He is playing ball with [boys of his own age] (equals).
He prefers playing to working. He likes playing better than work. He prefers play to work.
It is better to play when the weather is fine and [to read] (to apply oneself to letters) when it rains.
If the weather were fine, I would gladly play ball with you.
Do you like (does it please you) the ball game?
I like it, but today [it is pouring with rain] (it rains with stones): I prefer to read a book.
Let's go into the library! Here is a book you have never read!
